---
title: Designing view transitions
description: Learn how to use view transitions to communicate meaning during navigation, loading, and content changes in a Next.js app.
nav_title: View transitions
---

In web apps, route changes replace the entire page at once. One set of elements disappears, another appears, with no visual connection between them. A user selects a photo thumbnail to view it in detail on another page. They are the same image, but nothing on screen communicates that.

Apps that need these transitions typically rely on complex animation libraries that manage mount/unmount lifecycles, track element positions across routes, and coordinate timing manually, to animate how elements enter, exit, and move between states.

React's `<ViewTransition>` component integrates with the browser's [View Transitions API](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/View_Transition_API) to handle this declaratively. You name the elements that should persist, and the browser animates between their old and new positions.

This guide walks through four patterns that cover the most common cases: morphing shared elements, animating loading states, adding directional navigation, and crossfading content within the same route.

## Add view transitions with an agent

The [`vercel-react-view-transitions`](https://skills.sh/vercel-labs/agent-skills/vercel-react-view-transitions) skill teaches a coding agent the patterns in this guide, plus the CSS recipes and troubleshooting for applying them to an existing app.

The header stays fixed throughout both transitions. 00357| 00358| Browser-initiated back navigations (the back button or swipe gestures) do not carry a transition type, so the directional slide does not play. Morphs, reveals, and crossfades carry less risk since they affect smaller areas or rely on opacity rather than position. 00375| 00376| The simplest approach is to disable all animation durations: 00377| 00378| ```css filename="app/globals.css" 00379| @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) { 00380| ::view-transition-old(*), 00381| ::view-transition-new(*), 00382| ::view-transition-group(*) { 00383| animation-duration: 0s !important; 00384| animation-delay: 0s !important; 00385| } 00386| } 00387| ``` 00388| 00389| Without animation, content swaps instantly, which is the browser's default behavior. ---
title: Designing view transitions
description: Learn how to use view transitions to communicate meaning during navigation, loading, and content changes in a Next.js app.
nav_title: View transitions
---

In web apps, route changes replace the entire page at once. One set of elements disappears, another appears, with no visual connection between them. A user selects a photo thumbnail to view it in detail on another page. They are the same image, but nothing on screen communicates that.

Apps that need these transitions typically rely on complex animation libraries that manage mount/unmount lifecycles, track element positions across routes, and coordinate timing manually, to animate how elements enter, exit, and move between states.

React's `<ViewTransition>` component integrates with the browser's [View Transitions API](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/View_Transition_API) to handle this declaratively. You name the elements that should persist, and the browser animates between their old and new positions.

This guide walks through four patterns that cover the most common cases: morphing shared elements, animating loading states, adding directional navigation, and crossfading content within the same route.

## Add view transitions with an agent

The [`vercel-react-view-transitions`](https://skills.sh/vercel-labs/agent-skills/vercel-react-view-transitions) skill teaches a coding agent the patterns in this guide, plus the CSS recipes and troubleshooting for applying them to an existing app.

events.content:
View transitions have been added to the product gallery app:

- **Shared Element Morph:** Wrapped thumbnail images in `app/ProductGrid.tsx` and the detail hero image in `app/product/[slug]/page.tsx` with `<ViewTransition name={`product-${product.slug}`} share="morph" default="none">`.
- **Directional Navigation:** Added `transitionTypes={['nav-forward']}` to product links and `transitionTypes={['nav-back']}` to the back link, with page-level `<ViewTransition>` wrappers and directional slide CSS in `app/globals.css`.
- **Suspense Reveals:** Wrapped `<Suspense>` fallbacks (`exit="slide-down"`) and content (`enter="slide-up"`) in `<ViewTransition default="none">` on both pages.
- **Reduced Motion:** Added `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)` rules in `app/globals.css` to disable view transition animation durations and delays.

part.text:
View transitions have been added to the product gallery app:

- **Shared Element Morph:** Wrapped thumbnail images in `app/ProductGrid.tsx` and the detail hero image in `app/product/[slug]/page.tsx` with `<ViewTransition name={`product-${product.slug}`} share="morph" default="none">`.
- **Directional Navigation:** Added `transitionTypes={['nav-forward']}` to product links and `transitionTypes={['nav-back']}` to the back link, with page-level `<ViewTransition>` wrappers and directional slide CSS in `app/globals.css`.
- **Suspense Reveals:** Wrapped `<Suspense>` fallbacks (`exit="slide-down"`) and content (`enter="slide-up"`) in `<ViewTransition default="none">` on both pages.
- **Reduced Motion:** Added `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)` rules in `app/globals.css` to disable view transition animation durations and delays.
